questions.question: What is the difference between a syntax error and an exception in Python?
questions.title: Syntax Errors vs Exceptions in Python
questions.direct_answer: A syntax error means Python cannot parse code into a valid program; an exception occurs while syntactically valid code is being executed.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether parsing failures are distinguished from failures during execution.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying every Python error can be caught by placing `try` around a line in the same file.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use `compile()` to explain the valid outer-program boundary clearly.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: A `SyntaxError` is raised while Python parses invalid source code.
A runtime exception happens after valid code begins executing.
Normal code in a malformed module cannot run a handler around its own parse failure.
Dynamically compiled source can report `SyntaxError` because another valid program performs the compilation.
Runtime exceptions may be caught only when the program has a meaningful recovery.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A syntax error and a runtime exception fail at different stages. A syntax error means Python cannot parse source into a valid code object, for example because a colon is missing or parentheses do not balance. Since the module has not started executing, a `try` statement written inside that malformed source cannot catch the problem.

An exception occurs while valid Python is running. Dividing by zero, converting `"ten"` with `int`, or opening a missing file are syntactically valid operations that may raise `ZeroDivisionError`, `ValueError`, or `FileNotFoundError`. Surrounding the particular runtime operation with an appropriate handler can recover or translate it.

There is one useful boundary case: a valid program can call `compile()` on source text and catch the `SyntaxError` raised while that separate text is parsed. Tools such as editors and template systems use this pattern. It does not mean malformed application source can handle itself. The distinction is therefore parse time versus execution time, and recovery depends on whether another valid program is already running.

sections.title: Python must build code before it can run code
sections.content:
Parsing checks whether tokens follow Python's grammar. On failure, `SyntaxError` normally includes a filename, line number, offset, and source text to locate the problem. No statement in that source has executed yet.

Execution begins only after compilation succeeds. Runtime exceptions carry a traceback showing the active call stack, because functions and expressions were actually running. The exception type describes the failed operation and can travel outward through calling functions until a compatible handler is found.

Importing a malformed module also produces `SyntaxError` in the importing program. The importer may catch it, but the malformed module itself never reached its first statement. This stage model explains which code can possibly respond.

sections.title: Failure stage and available evidence
sections.content:
| Property | Syntax error | Runtime exception |
|---|---|---|
| Stage | Parsing or compilation | Execution |
| Example | Missing `:` | `10 / 0` |
| Did the failing source run? | No | Yes, up to the failing operation |
| Main location evidence | Line and offset | Stack traceback |
| Can surrounding valid code catch it? | Yes, when compiling or importing that source | Yes |

questions.question: What is the difference between bare except, except Exception, and a specific except clause?
questions.title: Bare except vs except Exception vs Specific Handling
questions.direct_answer: A specific clause catches one expected family, `except Exception` catches ordinary failures broadly, and bare `except` also intercepts exit and interrupt signals.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether handler breadth is connected to hierarchy, control signals, and truthful recovery.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using bare `except` to make errors disappear or treating a fabricated value as success.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Choose the narrowest complete policy and use cleanup constructs for cleanup.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: A specific clause gives the safest and most meaningful recovery boundary.
`except Exception` catches ordinary errors and custom `Exception` subclasses.
Bare `except` catches every `BaseException` branch, including interrupts and exits.
A broad boundary must log, translate, or terminate honestly rather than silently continue.
Cleanup that must run for all exits usually belongs in `finally` instead of a bare handler.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The three handler forms cover different portions of Python's exception hierarchy. A specific clause such as `except FileNotFoundError` catches that class and its subclasses, making it suitable when the program knows the exact failure and can perform the right recovery. `except Exception` catches most normal application and library errors, including custom errors derived from `Exception`, but it intentionally does not catch system-exiting types such as `KeyboardInterrupt` and `SystemExit`. A bare `except` catches those as well because it matches the whole `BaseException` tree.

For example, a settings loader may return defaults for a missing optional file, so `FileNotFoundError` is meaningful. A top-level worker boundary may use `except Exception` to log an unexpected job failure and mark the job failed, but it must not return a fake successful result. A bare handler could prevent Ctrl+C from stopping a command-line program, which is usually surprising and harmful.

If all paths need cleanup, `finally` or a context manager expresses that requirement without pretending to handle the failure. If a truly broad handler is required for emergency logging, it should normally re-raise after recording evidence.

The practical choice is the narrowest type for which this layer has a complete policy. Specific handling supports recovery, an `Exception` boundary supports controlled reporting, and bare handling is reserved for rare cases that deliberately include interpreter control signals.

sections.title: The width of a handler changes program control
sections.content:
Broad catching is not merely less detailed logging. It changes which requests to stop or exit the program are allowed to travel. `KeyboardInterrupt` represents a user interrupt, and `SystemExit` is raised by `sys.exit()`. Their placement outside `Exception` protects them from routine application handlers.

A handler is complete only when it establishes a truthful next state. Returning an empty list after a database outage is not recovery if an empty list means that no records exist. Valid actions include using a documented fallback, translating to a boundary-specific error, rolling back work, or reporting failure and stopping that unit of work.

Keep the protected suite narrow even with a specific type. The same exception class can be raised by multiple operations for different reasons. A narrow suite identifies which operation the handler intends to own and leaves unexpected failures visible.

sections.title: Handler width across the hierarchy
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  B[bare except: BaseException] --> E[except Exception]
  B --> K[KeyboardInterrupt / SystemExit]
  E --> O[except OSError]
  E --> V[except ValueError]
  O --> F[except FileNotFoundError]
  style F fill:#eef7f0,stroke:#5f7f68
  style E fill:#f6f2e8,stroke:#8a7855
  style B fill:#f7eeee,stroke:#976b6b
```
